evidence.claim: The U.S. Department of Defense reported the assessment that Putin placed Russian nuclear deterrence forces on special alert on 27 February 2022.
evidence.title: Russian strategic forces reportedly on high alert
evidence.source_locator: HTML article discussion of 27 February alert.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official defense statement reporting an assessment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly linked to Putin’s announced order, with posture details externally assessed.

evidence.claim: IAEA reported explosions near Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, damage to systems and equipment, and urgent need for a nuclear-safety zone.
evidence.title: IAEA statement on situation in Ukraine
evidence.excerpt: IAEA update on explosions and safety conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Conditions at a Russian-controlled facility; immediate actor attribution unresolved.
contrary_evidence: IAEA also reported no critical damage or casualties in the incident.

evidence.claim: The same IAEA update reported no critical damage or casualties in the cited Zaporizhzhia incident.
evidence.title: IAEA incident assessment
evidence.excerpt: IAEA caveat on damage and casualties.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Same primary technical report, distinct claim.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Facility-condition evidence; not direct ruler conduct.

evidence.claim: UN Security Council coverage recorded IAEA’s very alarming assessment, Russian control of the plant, and interference with Ukrainian and IAEA duties.
evidence.title: Security Council coverage of Zaporizhzhia situation
evidence.excerpt: Security Council coverage of IAEA concerns.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Russian control and institutional responsibility; not every technical act personally attributable.

evidence.claim: HRW documented Project Media’s designation as undesirable and related pressure on anti-corruption scrutiny.
evidence.title: World Report 2022: Russia
evidence.excerpt: World Report account of media and anti-corruption pressure.
evidence.source_locator: HTML Russia chapter sections on media and civil society.

evidence.claim: Arms Control Association reported uncertainty about the effects of the 27 February alert on nuclear forces and command-and-control, recorded Grom 2022 exercises, and noted reduced prospects for post-New START arms control.
evidence.title: Putin orders Russian nuclear weapons to higher alert
evidence.ruler_attribution: State-level strategic policy context; internal command attribution unresolved.

evidence.claim: Russia notified the United States under New START before testing an ICBM; DoD described the test as routine and not a threat.
evidence.title: Statement regarding Russian ICBM test
evidence.excerpt: DoD statement on Russian ICBM notification and test.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Russian state arms-control compliance; personal order not established.

evidence.claim: UNODA recorded New START as the principal strategic-arms limitation framework, with incomplete implementation because of inspection disagreements.
evidence.title: UNODA Yearbook 2022
evidence.excerpt: UNODA Yearbook discussion of New START.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional arms-control record; personal causation unresolved.

evidence.claim: IAEA’s September 2022 Ukraine report records safeguards implementation, seven nuclear-safety and security pillars, Chornobyl findings, and the need for a protection zone.
evidence.title: Ukraine: IAEA report
evidence.ruler_attribution: Russian-controlled facility conditions and state responsibility; internal command safeguards not established.

evidence.claim: The five NPT nuclear-weapon states, including Russia, stated on 3 January 2022 that nuclear war cannot be won or fought and that proliferation should be prevented.
evidence.title: Nuclear-weapon states reject nuclear war
evidence.source_locator: HTML article discussion of January 2022 statement.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Formal statement reported by specialist source.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Formal state statement; personal later compliance not established.
contrary_evidence: This formal statement does not establish later compliance.

evidence_environment.criticism_possible: Criticism was possible through international organizations, human-rights monitors, election monitors, technical agencies, and public diplomatic records, but domestic criticism was materially constrained. Supported by E001-E003, E007-E011, E015-E016, E021-E029, E035-E038, E047, E049-E052.
evidence_environment.censorship_and_self_censorship: Freedom House, HRW, Amnesty, OVD-Info, and OHCHR material documents censorship, media blocking, foreign-agent or extremist pressure, restricted assembly, and intimidation; these conditions create substantial self-censorship and suppress adverse domestic reporting. Supported by E008-E011, E025-E029, E040-E041.
evidence_environment.safe_reporting_channels: International organizations, foreign-based media, human-rights monitors, election monitors, technical agencies, and public international diplomatic records provided safer reporting channels than domestic independent media. Domestic media and civil-society channels were constrained by the laws and blocking documented in E008, E026-E027, E040-E041.
evidence_environment.official_statistics_reliability: Official statistics and formal records are usable for recorded outputs and macroeconomic conditions but require revision, definition, self-report, and distributional caveats. Rosstat’s revised and unrevised poverty figures differ; Russian Government and Social Fund claims lack independent implementation verification. Supported by E033, E043-E046, E053-E055.
languages_and_archives_searched: English-language UN, OHCHR, IAEA, ICRC, HRW, Freedom House, Amnesty, OVD-Info, IMF, World Bank, WHO, CSIS, ACA, Treasury, OCCRP, DoD, UNODA, State Department, Golos, Rosstat, Bank of Russia, Russian Government, and Social Fund materials.
Russian official government, budget, statistical, central-bank, legal, and Social Fund pages were included where supplied by the researcher.
evidence_environment.source_concentration: Evidence is concentrated among UN/OHCHR, HRW, Freedom House, Amnesty, ICRC, IMF, World Bank, IAEA, and official Russian institutions. Source-family diversity improved through ACA, CSIS, OVD-Info, Golos, OCCRP, Treasury, DoD, UNODA, Rosstat, and Bank of Russia, but several chapters remain monitor- and repression-heavy.
evidence_environment.duplicate_event_risk: Same-source claim families were identified: E006/E018, E019/E020, E021/E039, E026/E040, E027/E041, E034/E046, and E043-E045. These are retained with canonical-key warnings or context disposition and must not be counted as independent corroboration.
evidence_environment.complaint_volume_interpretation: International attention and open reporting overrepresent visible Ukraine-war, opposition, and media cases, while censorship and intimidation suppress less visible complaints. Aggregate welfare indicators may understate unequal hardship rather than complaint severity. Supported by E003, E008-E011, E021-E023, E025-E029, E038-E039, E053-E055.
evidence_environment.relevant_denominators: Relevant denominators include Russia’s population and affected civilian, prisoner, protester, household, regional, and beneficiary populations. The supplied local prior records population LF045; several narrative sources report counts without complete national or exposed-population denominators. This limits generalization.
evidence_environment.inherited_conditions_shocks_and_authorit: Putin’s formal authority is documented by E063. The 2022 invasion, mobilization, attempted annexation, occupation, sanctions, resource dependence, inherited institutional conditions, and pre-existing conflict are confounders across chapters. Local priors are explicitly context rather than direct ruler conduct.
chapter_specific_biases: 1B is affected mainly by secrecy, opaque command structures, and limited technical access.
2B is concentrated on the Ukraine war; battlefield visibility and restricted access jointly distort coverage.
3B is affected by suppressed complaints, prison-access limits, and weak remedy visibility.
4B is concentrated on repression and censorship, with incomplete electoral, judicial, and regional evidence.
5B and 6B rely heavily on aggregate or official statistics that can hide distributional and implementation differences.
7B has a very high personal-attribution risk; network and sanctions evidence must not be converted into proven ownership or criminal liability.
8B is confounded by war, sanctions, inherited capacity, and incomplete program-level implementation evidence.
